project.name: The Lexicon Deck
project.purpose: A reflective vocabulary of 22 images and phrases, inviting a reader to notice a situation and choose a thoughtful response.
project.audience: Adults interested in reflective and creative practice.

cards.title: THE THRESHOLD
cards.aphorism:
Step into the unknown,
readiness will follow.
cards.meaning: Use The Threshold as an invitation to consider beginning, rather than as a prediction. The card says: “Step into the unknown, readiness will follow.” Here, the image of a star above a doorway and ascending orange steps offers a starting point for noticing your own associations. Your own associations are part of the reading. Describe what you notice before deciding what it means for you. Keep the interpretation provisional and grounded in your circumstances.
cards.symbolism: a star above a doorway and ascending orange steps
cards.reflection: What small beginning could I make before I feel ready?
cards.practice: Choose one reversible step and write what you will learn from it.
cards.cautions: Reflection can support a choice; it does not establish facts about other people or replace appropriate professional support. You may skip any exercise.

sections.title: Welcome to The Lexicon Deck
sections.body: This deck invites you to pause, notice and respond. Its 22 images offer a vocabulary for beginning, recognising patterns, making choices and observing change. Start with an image or a phrase that draws your attention. You do not need to arrive with a finished question.

sections.title: A note to the reader
sections.body: Your interpretation belongs to you. Let each card begin a conversation rather than close it. You can work with one card for several days or return to a familiar image when your circumstances change. Keep what helps and set aside what does not.

sections.title: How to use this deck
sections.body: Choose a question about your own experience or a decision within your influence. Look at the image before reading the interpretation. Write down what you notice, then consider the reflection and practice. Return to your notes later to see what changed.

sections.title: Preparing your space
sections.body: Find a moment when you can attend to your question. Put the card where you can see it and keep a notebook nearby. A short pause may be enough. There is no need to force insight or complete every exercise.

sections.title: Reading an image
sections.body: Describe colour, shape, light and movement before assigning meaning. Notice where your eye goes first. An observation such as “the steps lead into darkness” can coexist with several interpretations. Record your association as a possibility, not a fact.

sections.title: Working with one card
sections.body: Read its title and short phrase. Let the reflection question open your own response. Choose a small practical action if one feels useful, and give yourself permission to stop or return another day.

sections.title: Working with three cards
sections.body: Try three positions: what I notice, what I need to consider, and a possible next step. Read each card on its own before connecting them. Different combinations may suggest different questions; they do not guarantee an outcome.

sections.title: Keeping a reflection journal
sections.body: Date your notes and include the card title, your question, an observation and a possible action. Keep private details in your own journal. When returning to a reading, note what you learned rather than judging whether you interpreted it correctly.

sections.title: A vocabulary for reflection
sections.body: Observation describes what you notice. Association records a personal connection. Interpretation proposes a meaning. Practice is an action you choose. Review means returning to what you wrote and considering what changed.

sections.title: Care and boundaries
sections.body: These exercises support reflection and creative attention. They do not establish facts about another person or replace appropriate professional advice. You may skip a prompt, change its wording or take a break.

sections.title: Closing reflection
sections.body: Return to the image that first drew you in. What do you notice now? Choose one thought to carry forward and one question to leave open. You do not need a final answer for the encounter to be useful.

worksheets.title: Set an intention
worksheets.body:
Write a question that gives you room to explore. Keep it connected to your experience and choices.

## Reflection prompts

What do I know? What am I assuming? What would a useful next step look like?

## A response to consider

I want to begin the guidebook without deciding its final length. I can test one short entry and see what it makes possible.

worksheets.title: A card response
worksheets.body:
Choose one card and describe the image before reading further. Separate observation, association and interpretation.

## Reflection prompts

What catches my attention? What does it remind me of? Which interpretation is useful today?

## A response to consider

With The Threshold, I notice ascending steps and an open doorway. I associate them with beginning before everything is known.

worksheets.title: A three-card conversation
worksheets.body:
Use three cards for context, a question and a possible action. Connect them in your own words.

## Reflection prompts

Where do the images agree? Where do they challenge each other? What remains uncertain?

## A response to consider

The Threshold, The Mirror and The Witness invite me to begin, notice my reaction to feedback and describe it before drawing conclusions.

worksheets.title: Build a personal vocabulary
worksheets.body:
Choose a word from an encounter with a card. Write a working meaning and allow it to change.

## Reflection prompts

Where did I first meet this word? What does it mean in this situation? How might I use it differently later?

## A response to consider

Readiness: enough clarity to try a reversible step. I do not need to know the whole path to begin.

worksheets.title: Make a creative decision
worksheets.body:
Name a decision and the alternatives you can reasonably try. Choose a small experiment.

## Reflection prompts

What is the decision? Which assumptions can I test? When will I review the result?

## A response to consider

I will compare a short reflection with a longer essay. My test is whether either leaves room for the reader’s own response.

worksheets.title: Return and notice change
worksheets.body:
Revisit a previous card response. Compare what you wrote then with what is present now.

## Reflection prompts

What changed? What stayed? What do I now see more clearly?

## A response to consider

The original question still matters, but I can now name the next action more precisely. I will return after trying it.

worksheets.title: Read with another person
worksheets.body:
Agree what you are comfortable sharing. Listen without telling the other person what their experience must mean.

## Reflection prompts

What is ours to discuss? What should stay private? What support or boundary would help?

## A response to consider

We agreed to discuss a creative decision and leave personal identifying details out of our shared notes.

worksheets.title: Bring the session to a close
worksheets.body:
Review your notes. Choose one useful action, one open question and a realistic time to return.

## Reflection prompts

What will I do? What can remain unanswered? When will I check in?

## A response to consider

I will draft one paragraph this week and then reconsider the question. The unfinished parts can stay open.

chapters.name: The Spark
chapters.label: Purpose of this deck
chapters.body: A reflective vocabulary of 22 images and phrases, inviting a reader to notice a situation and choose a thoughtful response.

chapters.name: The Foundation
chapters.label: Audience and experience
chapters.body: Adults who enjoy image-led reflection and want a gentle structure for creative attention. The voice should be clear, spacious and invitational.

chapters.name: The Architecture
chapters.label: Structure and relationships
chapters.body: Twenty-two cards, numbered 0–21. The sequence is preserved. Three working families organise beginnings and recognition, direction and discernment, and change and perspective.

chapters.name: The Expression
chapters.label: Card writing
chapters.body: Each card has a title, a source phrase, core meaning, symbolism, a reflection question and a practice. The recurring structure connects the card editor to the manuscript.

chapters.name: The Visual World
chapters.label: Visual direction
chapters.body: Geometric images, saturated teal, deep shadows and warm gold/orange light create continuity. Preserve the original aspect ratio and lettering while reviewing text separately.

chapters.name: The Companion
chapters.label: Reader-facing writing
chapters.body: Welcome pages lead into the 22 card entries. Reflection worksheets follow the card sequence and offer space for the reader’s own response.

chapters.name: The Making
chapters.label: Cards, guidebook and packaging
chapters.body: Planned card count: 22. Consider a printed guidebook and a digital reading copy. Card dimensions, stock, packaging and supplier proofs remain production decisions; preserve original image files throughout.

chapters.name: Into the World
chapters.label: Audience and release
chapters.body: Begin with a small demonstration and gather feedback on clarity and reading order. Prepare a coherent manuscript before choosing a publishing route. The creator contracts with and pays any suppliers directly.

journal.title: What this deck could make possible
journal.body: I want the demonstration to show a coherent relationship between a card, a reflection and an exercise. I will refine this purpose as I work.

journal.title: What still needs definition
journal.body: The images provide titles and aphorisms. I will develop the guidebook and the exercises with care, keeping a record of my decisions.

journal.title: Connecting the workbook
journal.body: I tested The Threshold with a small action prompt. I will ask the reviewer whether the prompt opens reflection without promising an outcome.

guidance.consultation_note: Discuss the recurring guidebook structure and how each card entry connects with a reflection practice.
guidance.review_note: Review The Threshold, The Mirror and The Witness for a consistent voice and a clear distinction between observation and interpretation.
guidance.feedback: Keep the source phrase intact, then let the reflection invite the reader’s own response. Separate what can be observed from the meaning you propose. A focused question can do more than a definite conclusion.
guidance.revision: Replaced a predictive statement with an open question and added separate observation and interpretation fields.

community.title: Keeping The Lexicon Deck’s purpose focused
community.author: Lexicon Creator
community.body: The Threshold says “Step into the unknown, readiness will follow.” The Witness says “Observe without attachment.” I want the Creative North Star to make room for both beginning and observing. Is “pause, notice and choose a thoughtful next step” a clear enough purpose, without promising an answer?
community.reply: The useful decision is what the deck invites a reader to do. “Notice and choose” gives the introduction a focus without telling the reader what must happen. What would make you feel that the deck had helped?

fields.backgroundNotes: The 22 images and short card phrases are already present. I am clarifying the intention that will connect their guidebook entries.
fields.heart: A vocabulary of 22 images for pausing, noticing what matters and choosing a thoughtful next step.
fields.inspiration: The contrast between The Threshold and The Witness: one invites a beginning, the other a pause. I want the same purpose to make room for both.
fields.why: I want the reader to feel that a card can open a useful question without deciding the answer for them.
fields.experience: Enough clarity to name what they notice and choose one small action within their own influence.
fields.perspective: A strong image can begin a conversation without needing to explain everything.
fields.connection: A creative interest in the relationship between an image, a short phrase and the reader’s own language.
fields.expression: Curious and accompanied, with room to disagree or leave a question open.
fields.principles: Clarity, room for interpretation, respect for the reader’s agency and continuity with the original images and phrases.
fields.out_idea: A vocabulary of 22 images for pausing, noticing what matters and choosing a thoughtful next step.
fields.out_why: To offer useful questions without taking the reader’s choices away.
fields.out_contribution: An image-led approach, connected through clear language and open reflection.
fields.out_experience: A moment of recognition and one practical possibility to consider.
fields.out_principles: Preserve the original sequence and card phrases. Keep interpretations invitational rather than predictive.

fields.intention: A manageable pause for reflection, followed by a reader-chosen response.
fields.essential: The space for a reader to find their own meaning.
fields.people: An adult who enjoys images and wants a reflective practice without needing an established card-reading system.
fields.context: Independently, with one card and a notebook; the guidebook offers a gentle starting point.
fields.encounter: The image draws attention; the phrase opens a question; the practice offers a small, optional action.
fields.promise: An invitation to reflect, not certainty about another person or a guaranteed outcome.
fields.conventions: Distinguish observation, association, interpretation and practice.
fields.principles: Respect the reader’s agency and avoid presenting personal associations as facts.
fields.heart: The 22 source images, their phrases and a coherent reflective guidebook.
fields.exploring: The length of card entries and the role of the eight reflection exercises.
fields.deferred: Additional cards, expanded editions or a facilitated course.
fields.responsibility: Confirm artwork and text credits before publication.
fields.questions: Does each entry leave enough room for the reader?
fields.out_people: Adults interested in images, reflection and creative attention.
fields.out_experience: Observe, consider and choose a small next step.
fields.out_principles: Agency, clarity and respect for uncertainty.
fields.out_scope: 22 cards, a guidebook and reflection exercises.
fields.out_questions: Test whether the reading order and entry lengths support the reader.

fields.form: A 22-card reflective deck, preserving the printed sequence 0–21 without claiming a full traditional tarot system.
fields.structure: Beginnings and recognition; direction and discernment; change and perspective. These are working families, not a change to the original sequence.
fields.contribution: The Threshold invites a beginning, while The Witness invites observation. Their difference helps define the range of the deck.
fields.balance: The Threshold and The Witness frame action and observation. The Mirror introduces a question about the response between them.
fields.use: Begin with one image, describe what is visible, then consider the phrase, reflection and practice.
fields.questions: Can every card stand alone while still contributing to the sequence?
fields.out_structure: Three working families; original sequence unchanged.
fields.out_balance: Beginning, recognition, choice and observation offer contrasting invitations.
fields.out_questions: Test entry lengths and the reading order with the intended audience.

fields.vision: A coherent geometric world of deep teal, warm orange and points of gold light.
fields.colour: Use the contrasts already present in the 22 source images.
fields.composition: Keep the central form visible and preserve the original portrait proportions.
fields.symbols: Doorways, paths, circles, stars and reflected light connect different invitations.
fields.treatment: Preserve the original images while reviewing their relationship to the writing.
fields.exceptions: Allow the image for each card to carry its own emphasis.

publication.subtitle: Words, images and a practice of reflection
publication.opening:
Begin with an image, a word and the situation you bring. This guidebook holds the twenty-two cards in their original sequence, alongside questions and small practices for returning attention to your own experience.

You can read a single entry, follow a chapter or use the reflection pages to keep a conversation with the deck over time. There is no requirement to find one final meaning. Let your observations remain specific, tentative and your own.
publication.framework:
The three chapters offer a way to move through the deck without turning its images into fixed answers. Begin by noticing what draws your attention, consider the choices available to you, then return to what has changed.

Read the card phrase beside the image before you read the interpretation. Distinguish what is visible from what you associate with it. A useful reading makes room for uncertainty and leads towards a small, thoughtful response.
publication.chapter1:
A threshold, a key, a vessel: beginnings ask us to notice the conditions of arrival. In these first seven cards, attend to what is opening, what needs care and what you recognise without yet having words for it.

Choose one image. Describe three things you can see, then name the question you would like to carry into the next chapter.
publication.chapter2:
The next eight cards invite discernment through connection, exchange and movement. Read the recurring thread between images while keeping their differences in view. What asks for tending, weighing, offering or releasing?

Write two possible responses to a situation. Ask what each one protects and what it might make possible. Choose a reversible experiment rather than a final verdict.
publication.chapter3:
The final seven cards bring attention to complexity, expression and perspective. A knot need not be forced open; a labyrinth can be walked one turn at a time. Notice what becomes clearer when you allow more than one viewpoint.

Return to your opening question. Record what changed, what remains unresolved and one action that fits the understanding you have now.
publication.exerciseIntroduction:
These pages are for your own words. Begin with a card, a situation and a question you can explore through experience. Write only what you want to keep; leave space for uncertainty and return later if a response changes.

The exercises move from intention and observation towards conversation, decision and closure. You can use them in order or choose the practice that fits your situation. A short, specific response is enough.
